etymologies.etymologyHTML: From Middle French défensif. Morphologically defense +‎ -ive.

definitions.definition: Performed so as to minimise risk.
Displaying an inordinate sensitivity to criticism or intrusion; oversensitive; thin-skinned.
(cricket) Of a bowling or fielding tactic designed to prevent the other side from scoring runs; of a batting tactic designed to prevent being out.
(chiefly sports) Pertaining to defense, as opposed to attack.

quote.citation: 2011 September 2, Phil McNulty, “Bulgaria 0-3 England”, in BBC‎[1]:
quote.text: The Italian opted for Bolton's Cahill alongside captain John Terry - and his decision was rewarded with a goal after only 13 minutes. Bulgaria gave a hint of defensive frailties to come when they failed to clear Young's corner, and when Gareth Barry found Cahill in the box he applied the finish past Nikolay Mihaylov.

definitions.definition: In a state or posture of defense.

quote.citation: 1671, John Milton, “Samson Agonistes, […].”, in Paradise Regain’d. A Poem. In IV Books. To which is Added, Samson Agonistes, London:  […]  J[ohn] M[acock] for John Starkey […], →OCLC, pages 63–64, lines 48–49:
quote.text: […] Once join'd, the contrary ſhe proves, a thorn Inteſtin, far within defenſive arms […]

definitions.definition: A means, attitude or position of defense.

quote.citation: 2007 May 26, Julia Werdigier, “Consolidating the Banks of Europe”, in New York Times‎[2]:
quote.text: Such kinds of defensives are really rather protecting the local companies than the consumers.
